## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Gaṅgeyyajātaka* (Ja 205) is a short birth story found in the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1879]. According to its introductory framework, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana, directed toward two young monks (*dahara-bhikkhū*) [Fausböll 1879]. These two young men from Sāvatthī had entered the monastic order, but instead of devoting themselves to meditation on bodily unattractiveness (*asubhabhāvanā*), they became enamored with and constantly praised their own good looks [Fausböll 1879].

To curb their vanity, the Buddha related a tale of their past lives. The single canonical verse of the jātaka (opening with the *pratīka* *Sobhanti macchā gaṅgeyyā*) notes that while the fish of the Ganges and the fish of the Yamunā are both handsome, a four-footed creature rounded like a banyan tree with a slightly extended neck outshines them all [Fausböll 1879; Fausböll 1897]. This boastful claim was made by a tortoise seeking to proclaim his own superior beauty; disgusted by his ugliness and arrogance, the two fish splashed water over him and swam away [Fausböll 1879]. In the resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the two fish as the two young monks, the tortoise as an elderly monk (*mahallaka*), and the tree deity on the bank of the Ganges who witnessed the event as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].
